faqs.q: How long does a typical project take?
faqs.a: A focused prototype can take a few weeks; a production application usually takes several months. We give you a timeline after discovery, broken into milestones you can review.

faqs.q: How is pricing decided?
faqs.a: We price each engagement after discovery, once the scope, timeline, and responsibilities are clear. You receive a written proposal before any commitment.

faqs.q: Who owns the software and data?
faqs.a: Ownership of code, data, and deliverables is set out in the agreement before work starts. As a default, we propose that you own the solution built for you and all of your data.

faqs.q: How do you handle security?
faqs.a: Security is treated as a requirement from discovery onward: least-privilege access, secure configuration, input validation, dependency updates, and security testing before launch.

faqs.q: What happens after launch?
faqs.a: We train your administrators and users, then offer support and maintenance so the product stays secure and keeps improving.

faqs.q: What do you need from us to start?
faqs.a: A short description of the problem, who will use the solution, and any existing systems or documents. A brief is helpful but not required.

cta.label: Discuss Your Software Project
cta.heading: Tell us about the product you need.
cta.body: Share the problem, your users, and any constraints. We'll reply with next steps and, where it helps, a short discovery call.

Workflows that must change to benefit from the system

insights.title: Preparing for a system implementation: a practical checklist
insights.summary: Most system projects succeed or fail before configuration starts. Here is what to prepare before you introduce or replace a system.
insights.author: Novatrix Team

body.text: Introducing a new system is an organizational change, not only a technical one. The preparation you do before configuration starts has the biggest influence on whether people adopt it.
1. Agree the outcome
Write down the problem the system should solve and how you will know it worked. Measures such as time saved per request, fewer errors, or faster reporting keep decisions focused.
2. Map how work happens today
Document the current process, including workarounds. A system configured around an unclear process simply digitizes the confusion.
3. Review your data early

items: List every data source that must move to the new system
Check completeness, duplicates, and inconsistent formats
Decide what historical data is actually needed
Name an owner who can approve data decisions

body.text: 4. Plan training from the start
Budget time for role-based training, documentation, and support during go-live. Adoption is part of implementation, not a follow-up task.
5. Decide how you will support it
Agree who handles user questions, updates, backups, and improvements after launch, and how issues are escalated.

insights.title: Custom software or off-the-shelf: how to decide
insights.summary: Building custom software is not always the right answer. A few questions help you decide between building, buying, and configuring.
insights.author: Novatrix Team

body.text: Organizations often ask whether they should build a custom application or buy an existing product. The honest answer depends on how unique your process is and how much control you need.
Buy or configure when

items: Your process is standard, such as accounting or payroll
A mature product already meets most of your requirements
You need to launch quickly with a limited budget

body.text: Build when

items: Your process is a differentiator for your organization
You need tight integration with other systems or full data control

body.text: Consider a combination
Many successful solutions configure an existing platform for standard work and add custom components or integrations where they create value.
Whichever route you choose, plan for training and ongoing support. Software only creates value when people use it confidently.

insights.title: Planning corporate technology training that changes how teams work
insights.summary: Effective workforce training starts with clear objectives and ends with evidence. A simple framework for planning your next program.
insights.author: Novatrix Team

body.text: Training budgets are easiest to justify when programs are linked to specific work outcomes and when sponsors can see what participants learned.
Start with a needs assessment
Survey participants and managers to understand current skills, tools, and the tasks people struggle with. Group participants by role or level so sessions stay relevant.
Make it practical
Use exercises based on the tools and data your team actually uses. Practical tasks build confidence faster than slides.
Measure and report

items: Assessment results based on practical tasks
